subtype: Sharing tasks in a student group [Actor]
passage: At the polytechnic in the small town, Anand gave each group member a piece of the project on a slip of paper and said, “Bring it when it's done.” No date, no check-in. Ojas got the wiring diagram and kept it in a notebook, meaning to start. Three others worked with quiet resentment, since Anand had kept the best part, the model, for himself. A week later Anand asked who had finished. Only two hands went up. Ojas had not started, and now felt embarrassed and stayed away from the lab. Anand stared at the empty slot in the plan, at the model that lacked wires, and understood that he had handed out jobs but no way of knowing how they were going.

qa.q: What did Ojas get from Anand?
qa.a: Ojas got the wiring diagram.

qa.q: Why did Ojas stay away from the lab?
qa.a: Ojas had not started and felt embarrassed, and avoiding the lab was easier than facing the group.

qa.q: What could Anand do now to rescue the project?
qa.a: Sit with Ojas, agree a small first step and one date, and set a shared check-in for the whole group.

qa.q: How might the other three group members feel about how the work was split?
qa.a: They probably feel resentful, since Anand kept the best part, and unsure how their own pieces fit, because there was no check-in.

grounding: A group leader hands out pieces with no check-in, so members resent the load or vanish.

subtype: Sharing tasks in a student group [Actor]
passage: Anders was chosen to lead his group's marketing project at university in Copenhagen. Four members, three weeks. The first week, he did the research, wrote the outline and designed the slides himself. "It's faster," he told himself. By week two he was exhausted and snapping at people. Daniel, one of the members, said, "You never gave us anything to do. Then you complain that we don't help." Anders felt a flash of anger, then embarrassment. That evening he split the rest: Daniel on the survey, the others on case studies and the budget. Each piece had one name. They agreed on one checkpoint on Friday. On Friday, everyone arrived with their part.

qa.q: How many members were in Anders's group?
qa.a: There were four members.

qa.q: What did Anders feel when Daniel spoke up?
qa.a: He felt a flash of anger, then embarrassment, recognising that he had kept all the work himself.

qa.q: Which change worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving each piece one owner and agreeing on one Friday checkpoint made the split clear, so everyone arrived with their part.

qa.q: How did Daniel see the first two weeks?
qa.a: Daniel felt shut out and unfairly blamed, since Anders gave no tasks but complained about the lack of help.

grounding: Shows a group leader who took everything himself, then splits tasks with clear owners and one checkpoint.

subtype: Sharing tasks in a student group [Actor]
passage: In the college seminar room, Amandeep, leader of the five-person group project on urban transport, had sent a message on day one: "Everyone pick a section and do it." Then nothing. Two weeks later, at the first meeting, only Charu had written anything, and it overlapped with a section Amandeep had assumed was someone else's. Two members hadn't opened the document. One had left the group chat. Charu sighed. "I did my part and half of someone else's." Amandeep's stomach dropped. He wrote each section on the whiteboard, put one name next to each and said, "Let's meet here on Thursday at four. Bring a draft, even a rough one."

qa.q: How many members were in Amandeep's project group?
qa.a: There were five members.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when he saw how little had been done?
qa.a: His stomach dropped; he felt worried and guilty, realising his loose instruction had left the work unowned.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do to fix the split?
qa.a: He wrote each section with one name next to it and set a single Thursday checkpoint for rough drafts.

qa.q: How does Charu feel about the first two weeks?
qa.a: Charu feels resentful and tired, having done her part and half of someone else's.

grounding: Shows a group leader who handed out work with no owners or check-in, then fixes it with clear names and one checkpoint.

subtype: Sharing tasks in a student group [Actor]
passage:
Dear Tanvir,

I'm writing because I owe you an apology, and a plan. When I became leader of our history project, I just said "divide it among yourselves" and disappeared into my own section. I thought I was being relaxed. What happened: you did three sections, Lalitha did none, and nobody knew who had the bibliography.

I know you're angry, and you're right to be.

Here's what I'd like to do. I've made a table: each of us has one section and one extra job. I've put your name only on the conclusion. We'll all meet once, on Monday at 1 p.m., in the library to check where we are.

Gargi

qa.q: How many sections did Tanvir end up doing?
qa.a: Tanvir did three sections.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel about the way the project was led?
qa.a: Gargi feels guilty and apologetic, recognising that a loose instruction left Tanvir with too much.

qa.q: What does Gargi's new plan fix?
qa.a: The table gives each person one section and one extra job, and the Monday meeting is a single agreed checkpoint.

qa.q: How has Tanvir been affected so far?
qa.a: Tanvir has been angry and overloaded, carrying three sections while others did none.

grounding: A group leader's letter admits handing out work with no owners or check-in, and proposes clear owners and one checkpoint.

subtype: Sharing tasks in a student group [Actor]
passage: "Rehana, I've led a group twice this year and got it wrong both ways. I'm Irawati, by the way, for your listeners. First, the lake survey. I did the water samples, the photos, the report, even the bibliography. The others kept asking, 'What should we do?' and I kept saying, 'It's fine, I've got it.' By the end I was in tears over the printer, and Tushar told the professor he'd barely been allowed to help. He wasn't wrong. So for the street-play project I swung the other way. I sent one message: 'Script, props, posters, permissions. Pick one, bring it on the day.' No date to check in. Two people picked nothing and went quiet. The posters turned up on the morning of the show, spelled wrong. Next time I want one name next to each job, and one Friday where we all show what we've got."

qa.q: What did Irawati's message for the street-play project list?
qa.a: Script, props, posters and permissions: pick one, bring it on the day.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel at the end of the lake survey?
qa.a: Irawati was exhausted and overwhelmed, ending up in tears over the printer after doing every part alone.

qa.q: What went wrong both times, and what could fix it?
qa.a: First Irawati kept all the work, then handed it out with no check-in; clear owners for each job and one agreed checkpoint would fix both.

qa.q: How did Tushar see the lake survey?
qa.a: Tushar felt shut out and resentful, telling the professor he had barely been allowed to help.

grounding: Shows a student group leader who first takes on everything and then hands out pieces with no check-in, leading to resentment and members vanishing.
